messages.subject: RNG input validation --- to Boost Policy or not?
messages.subject_clean: RNG input validation --- to Boost Policy or not?
messages.body_plain:
We need to

   * validate inputs for the RNG functions, and

   * add unit tests for invalid inputs.

For instance, the bernoulli_rng(theta) function should validate
that 0 <= theta <= 1 and take action otherwise.

But what action?  There are three options I could live
with:

   1.  Just throw an exception in the function if the input is illegal,

   2.  Go the full Boost error-handling route, or

   3.  Use a single static/singleton Boost Policy everywhere.

We should make this decision and then

   * add validation for all of our functions

The upside of just throwing is that it's easier to write,
easier to doc, easier to test, and it's faster to compile.

The downside of just throwing is that we can't configure for
clients who don't want exceptions.

An in between solution is to only use a single static
singleton policy anywhere that could be configured by
a client.  This is like always going with the "default policy".
Right now, that's the behavior of our functions with
no explicit Policy argument.

Thoughts?

- Bob

messages.subject: error handling decision
messages.body_plain:
I think we should

   * configure error handling policy globally for all of
     the functions in Stan (we can use Boost's global policy
     or customize it in a single location)

   * remove function signatures with explicit Policy
     template parameters & use global values

Step 2 cuts the number of function definitions in half
without invoking C++-11-only function template defaults.

I think we should also:

   * remove implicit propto=false probabilty functions and
     require explicit template parameter instantiation

The model code is already making propto specific, e.g. with
normal_log<false>(...).

Step 2 and 3 together take us back to one C++ templated
function signature per Stan function signature.  There may be
more than one implementation because of specializations for
auto-dif.

The change should be relatively easy and modular because
we'd be removing functionality we haven't used.

Let's finalize a decision in the meeting tomorrow.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob, thanks for getting these thoughts out. I'm inlining some thoughts.

On Mon, Apr 1, 2013 at 1:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I think we should
>
>   * configure error handling policy globally for all of
>     the functions in Stan (we can use Boost's global policy
>     or customize it in a single location)

That works for me. It will disable our ability to use policies to disable specific error checking in things like distributions calling other distributions, but I'm ok with this decision because it will simplify our code greatly. That and we haven't really had a need for configurable error handling.

>   * remove function signatures with explicit Policy
>     template parameters & use global values
>
> Step 2 cuts the number of function definitions in half
> without invoking C++-11-only function template defaults.

Yeah, that sounds good. It'll be easier to maintain and we can cut down on some of our tests.

> I think we should also:
>
>   * remove implicit propto=false probabilty functions and
>     require explicit template parameter instantiation

Yes! For those of you not following closely, this will change the C++ calls a little. This means calling normal_log(y, mu, sigma) will require a call like:
normal_log<true,true,true>(y, mu, sigma). This way we can drop appropriate proportionality constants in a more controlled fashion from the outside.

I'm not sure if the logic we used for determining when to compute gradients will still hold, but it's just a thought exercise that we need to walk through once, I think.

> The model code is already making propto specific, e.g. with
> normal_log<false>(...).
>
> Step 2 and 3 together take us back to one C++ templated
> function signature per Stan function signature.  There may be
> more than one implementation because of specializations for
> auto-dif.
>
> The change should be relatively easy and modular because
> we'd be removing functionality we haven't used.

Agreed. A little bit of work, but easy.

> Let's finalize a decision in the meeting tomorrow.
>

Unless someone has a compelling reason against doing this, my vote is for the suggestions that Bob has laid out.

> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] R-hat and n_eff for ragged chains?
messages.body_plain:
Let me make a concrete plan:

1.  User specifies a total run time t.

2.  We run warmup until the first iteration ending at a time past t/2.

3.  We then run sampling iterations until the first iteration past time t.

4.  Analyze ragged R-hat and n_eff with each chain weighted equally.

Is this what you (Andrew) had in mind?  If so, that's what
we can implement.  I don't think anyone else has a strong
opinion on how this should go.

I'm not sure what this'll do to computation compared to running
each chain the same number of iterations.

Timed setup:  If one chain is slow to converge in wall time,
the other chains will keep running for the same amount of time, which
they didn't technically need to do.

# Iterations condition:   If one chain takes more iterations to converge,
the other chains will have to keep running for that many iterations,
which they didn't technically need to do.

What we really want is to run until each chain has converged :-)

What I'm seeing in practice is that some chains are slow in wall
time because adaptation gets stuck, but by the time it gets unstuck,

Actually, let's think more about this.  Given that we are optimizing over global parameters, I think we should definitely be sharing info in the adaptation.  To start with, this means that when we're running standard serial Stan, we should not be doing all of chain 1, then all of chain 2, etc.  One approach would be to thread everything (i.e., 1 iteration of chain 1, 1 iteration of chain 2, 1 iteration of chain 3, etc), another approach would be to break it into blocks (10 of chain 1, 10 of chain 2, etc).

On Saturday, March 30, 2013 10:46:25 PM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
> I've finished implementing RNG for all of the current distributions (except for ikj corr and cov).

I did the lkj_corr yesterday. A few general comments on your other RNGs:

-- I think the arguments should be const qualified wherever possible, like

poisson_rng(double lambda, ...
->
poisson_rng(const double lambda, ...

-- Eigen's .inverse() method should be avoided in Stan because it does not take advantage of positive definiteness. So, it is a bit slow and also does not rigorously preserve symmetry. I think the best construction is to use a Cholesky decomposition, as in

S.inverse()
->
S_inv = Eigen::MatrixXd::Identity(S.cols(),S.cols());
S_inv = S.ldlt().solve(S_inv); // no additional malloc

-- There is a multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose() function for multiplying a lower triangular matrix by its own transpose that takes into account symmetry and sparsity that you can use when necessary, like

S.llt().matrixL() * B * B.transpose() * S.llt().matrixL().transpose();
->
multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(S.llt().matrixL() * B);

-- In wishart_rng, there is a

Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic> A(S.rows(), 1);

that is unused, and if it were used, it would be better to declare it as Eigen::VectorXd. Also, you can use the ::Zero(rows, cols) construction to allocate B with zeros rather than looping, see

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1DenseBase.html#a724349af3e253b69a54d503931b52ec3

Otherwise it looks good. Thanks for doing all of these.

Ben

differently.

are identical.  The const only controls whether you can reassign
the copy of the argument local to the function definition.

My inclination for primitive types is to follow the std lib,
which does NOT const qualify primitive arguments; e.g.,

 > For Eigen types, having the const serves another purpose

because of the strong distinction between row vectors,
column vectors and matrices.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiously_recurring_template_pattern

but I don't know there's much we can rely on in the Derived class.

messages.subject: Gaussian Processes in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I've been implementing a couple GP models in Stan recently and I've
come up with two issues I wanted to run past the list.

First, there is a need for a "GP distribution" in order to more
efficiently support multivariate GP outputs.  Basically, if you have a
vector valued function, people typically treat each output as
independent but with related hyperparameters (and thus, often the same
kernel matrix).  Right now in Stan this works out looking something
like:

  vector[N] y_trans[d];
  vector[d] w;
  matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
  matrix[N,N] Sigma;
...
  // Output likelihood
  for (i in 1:yDim) {
    // Compute the kernel matrix for this output
    Sigma <- w[i] * K_sqExp;
    y_trans[i] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
  }

where y_trans[i] is a vector containing the ith dimension of output
for each training point.  This is one of the common cases, where each
output dimension is given a different scale (w[i]) but the underlying
kernel matrix (K_sqExp) is shared.

I'm almost done implementing a multigp_log(y,Sigma,w) function which
would replace the above with:

  matrix[d,N] y;
  matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
  vector[d] w;
  y ~ multigp(K_sqExp,w);

Any comments or suggestions on this?  It might be more broadly useful
and, thus, should have a different name perhaps?  Should it be
generalized to handle parameter/kernel sharing types?

The other issue is that of repeated matrix factorizations in the
mdivide_left and log_determinant varis.  I'd like to create a single
"factorization" vari which can be used to solve linear systems,
compute determinants, etc and only ever factorize the matrix once.
Before that though, I'd just like to avoid repeatedly factorizing a
matrix at construction and in chain().  In principle this shouldn't be
hard, just stick an Eigen:LDLT<> object into the vari and we're done,
except it will never be deleted because of the vari memory management.
 I have two proposals for this.

1) Call some kind of vari cleanup function.  E.G., every vari has a
virtual cleanup() function  which is called when memory is freed.
This is simple to do, but will incur an overhead which will be rarely
needed since the cleanup() function will probably empty 99% of the
time.

2) Alternatively, when a vari is constructed that needs to be cleaned
up, it is added to a special list which is traversed at cleanup time.
This has the advantage of almost zero overhead, but increased
implementation complexity.

Any thoughts on these two approaches?  Is there an obvious alternative
that I'm missing?

I'm hoping to have most of this landed in the next few days unless
someone objects.

Cheers,
Marcus

The transform is described near the end of the manual in

for the transforms for variables read from

inverse transforms to constrained parameters and then
writes the real ones to an array.  This follows the
same format as write_csv(), writing the parameters out
in row-major order in the order they were declared.
The output is constrained.   write_csv_header() writes
out the "names" of the parameters, including the
indices of an array --- this is the header dumped out
in the output from the command.

them as an instant rejection.   They also did the same
thing with -infinity and NaN returns.

We have our functions configured with exceptions
so that then we can record an error message to report
when it's caught.

So far, the messages aren't very good, because they're
not located with respect to the user model -- they just
say which function was called and what the problem was
with the parameters it was called with.

To get better messages, we'd need to pass more information
to the functions from the model, such as the line number
of the call in the Stan model (not the C++ code).
Or we could dream up some alternative.  (For instance, we could
put a try/catch around every function call :-))

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
For timing, if it goes in independently and passes tests,
no big deal one way or the other.  Michael's in the middle
of refactoring the samplers, but those are orthogonal to
new functions and reimplemented vari.

1.  I have no opinion about which GP components are usefully
reusable.

As far as coding it, we're working on more general vector views.
But however you code it, we can translate it into the new framework
when we get there.

2.  As to saving the results of a solver, by all means.  Ben's
been wanting to do something like this for ages.

I prefer a separate stack of things to free.  Otherwise, it's
way too much overhead on top of auto-diff.

A virtual cleanup function is the elegant way to do this.  It'll
have a bit of extra overhead from the virtual function call over
just saving a stack of pointers to free.   Do we need the extra
generality?  Or is it worth it just to have the interfaces be
cleaner?

I don't think we'll be able to finagle Eigen's solvers to use
our memory, for instance by using a placement new, because
they're bound to be doing lower-level allocation for internal
matrices.

- Bob

messages.subject: boost headers and rstan
messages.body_plain:
Thinking again about how we could get RStan onto CRAN, if we made boost a system requirement to build stanc (only) and created a dependency on the BH package

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BH/index.html

in order to build both libstan and the user models, then I think we could avoid the purported reason (excessive size) that RStan was rejected the first time. There is an issue that the BH package is based on boost 1.51, but presumably we could ask Jay to update it and presumably we want Stan to stick with boost 1.51 for a while due to the ongoing modularization / git-ification of boost.

However, the BH package currently does not include enough of boost to build libstan or the user models. AFAICT, these headers (plus whatever they pull in) are needed by some part of (the master branch of) Stan but are not included in the BH package

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ cat /tmp/missing_boost_headers.txt
boost/accumulators/accumulators.hpp
boost/algorithm/string.hpp
boost/exception/all.hpp
boost/fusion/include/adapt_struct.hpp
boost/math/constants/constants.hpp
boost/math/distributions.hpp
boost/math/policies/error_handling.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/acosh.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/asinh.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/atanh.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/beta.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/cbrt.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/digamma.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/erf.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/gamma.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/hypot.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/owens_t.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/round.hpp
boost/math/special_functions/trunc.hpp
boost/multi_array.hpp
boost/random/additive_combine.hpp
boost/random/bernoulli_distribution.hpp
boost/random/binomial_distribution.hpp
boost/random/cauchy_distribution.hpp
boost/random/chi_squared_distribution.hpp
boost/random/exponential_distribution.hpp
boost/random/gamma_distribution.hpp
boost/random/lognormal_distribution.hpp
boost/random/negative_binomial_distribution.hpp
boost/random/normal_distribution.hpp
boost/random/poisson_distribution.hpp
boost/random/student_t_distribution.hpp
boost/random/uniform_01.hpp
boost/random/uniform_real_distribution.hpp
boost/random/weibull_distribution.hpp
boost/spirit/include/qi.hpp
boost/variant/apply_visitor.hpp
boost/variant/recursive_variant.hpp

I obtained this list by moving my /usr/include/boost out of the way and calling

make clean-all && make O=0 CC=clang++ BOOST=/tmp/BH/inst/include/ -j7 -k test-all 2> /tmp/boost_errors.txt
grep -F "file not found" /tmp/boost_errors.txt | sed 's/^.*error: //g' | sed 's/ file not found//g' | sort | uniq | sed s/\'//g > /tmp/missing_boost_headers.txt

Of the above, I suspect the following are "stanc only"

boost/fusion/include/adapt_struct.hpp
boost/spirit/include/qi.hpp
boost/variant/apply_visitor.hpp
boost/variant/recursive_variant.hpp

Is that correct? If I exclude those and use bcp to copy everything that the remaining headers pull in, it adds 8M of files that were not already in the BH package, which could be a problem for them so if it is possible to cut down further that would be good.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Gaussian Processes in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Ok, I've pushed some changes.  I've introduced a class called
chainable_alloc with a virtual destructor.  When a chainable_alloc is
created, a pointer to it is put on a new stack which is then deleted
in recover_memory().  One important note is that a chainable_alloc
object should *never* be created on the stack, only ever on the heap.

Before doing the full factorization function, I instead implemented a
mdivide_left_spd() function for solving symmetric positive definite
systems and then made use of it in multi_normal_log().  This function
should probably also be used in the wishart and  multi_student_t
distributions.

Next up, I'll finish implementing the multivariate GP function and
then I'll probably do the full factorization function for use in both
that and in multi_normal_log.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Apr 8, 2013 at 1:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> For timing, if it goes in independently and passes tests,
> no big deal one way or the other.  Michael's in the middle
> of refactoring the samplers, but those are orthogonal to
> new functions and reimplemented vari.
>
> 1.  I have no opinion about which GP components are usefully
> reusable.
>
> As far as coding it, we're working on more general vector views.
> But however you code it, we can translate it into the new framework
> when we get there.
>
> 2.  As to saving the results of a solver, by all means.  Ben's
> been wanting to do something like this for ages.
>
> I prefer a separate stack of things to free.  Otherwise, it's
> way too much overhead on top of auto-diff.
>
> A virtual cleanup function is the elegant way to do this.  It'll
> have a bit of extra overhead from the virtual function call over
> just saving a stack of pointers to free.   Do we need the extra
> generality?  Or is it worth it just to have the interfaces be
> cleaner?
>
> I don't think we'll be able to finagle Eigen's solvers to use
> our memory, for instance by using a placement new, because
> they're bound to be doing lower-level allocation for internal
> matrices.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 4/8/13 12:32 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>>
>> Hey everyone,
>>
>> I've been implementing a couple GP models in Stan recently and I've
>> come up with two issues I wanted to run past the list.
>>
>> First, there is a need for a "GP distribution" in order to more
>> efficiently support multivariate GP outputs.  Basically, if you have a
>> vector valued function, people typically treat each output as
>> independent but with related hyperparameters (and thus, often the same
>> kernel matrix).  Right now in Stan this works out looking something
>> like:
>>
>>    vector[N] y_trans[d];
>>    vector[d] w;
>>    matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
>>    matrix[N,N] Sigma;
>> ...
>>    // Output likelihood
>>    for (i in 1:yDim) {
>>      // Compute the kernel matrix for this output
>>      Sigma <- w[i] * K_sqExp;
>>      y_trans[i] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
>>    }
>>
>> where y_trans[i] is a vector containing the ith dimension of output
>> for each training point.  This is one of the common cases, where each
>> output dimension is given a different scale (w[i]) but the underlying
>> kernel matrix (K_sqExp) is shared.
>>
>> I'm almost done implementing a multigp_log(y,Sigma,w) function which
>> would replace the above with:
>>
>>    matrix[d,N] y;
>>    matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
>>    vector[d] w;
>>    y ~ multigp(K_sqExp,w);
>>
>> Any comments or suggestions on this?  It might be more broadly useful
>> and, thus, should have a different name perhaps?  Should it be
>> generalized to handle parameter/kernel sharing types?
>>
>>
>> The other issue is that of repeated matrix factorizations in the
>> mdivide_left and log_determinant varis.  I'd like to create a single
>> "factorization" vari which can be used to solve linear systems,
>> compute determinants, etc and only ever factorize the matrix once.
>> Before that though, I'd just like to avoid repeatedly factorizing a
>> matrix at construction and in chain().  In principle this shouldn't be
>> hard, just stick an Eigen:LDLT<> object into the vari and we're done,
>> except it will never be deleted because of the vari memory management.
>>   I have two proposals for this.
>>

>>>
>>> Hey everyone,
>>>
>>> I've been implementing a couple GP models in Stan recently and I've
>>> come up with two issues I wanted to run past the list.
>>>
>>> First, there is a need for a "GP distribution" in order to more
>>> efficiently support multivariate GP outputs.  Basically, if you have a
>>> vector valued function, people typically treat each output as
>>> independent but with related hyperparameters (and thus, often the same
>>> kernel matrix).  Right now in Stan this works out looking something
>>> like:
>>>
>>>     vector[N] y_trans[d];
>>>     vector[d] w;
>>>     matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
>>>     matrix[N,N] Sigma;
>>> ...
>>>     // Output likelihood
>>>     for (i in 1:yDim) {
>>>       // Compute the kernel matrix for this output
>>>       Sigma <- w[i] * K_sqExp;
>>>       y_trans[i] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
>>>     }
>>>
>>> where y_trans[i] is a vector containing the ith dimension of output
>>> for each training point.  This is one of the common cases, where each
>>> output dimension is given a different scale (w[i]) but the underlying
>>> kernel matrix (K_sqExp) is shared.
>>>
>>> I'm almost done implementing a multigp_log(y,Sigma,w) function which
>>> would replace the above with:
>>>
>>>     matrix[d,N] y;
>>>     matrix[N,N] K_sqExp;
>>>     vector[d] w;

>>> and, thus, should have a different name perhaps?  Should it be
>>> generalized to handle parameter/kernel sharing types?
>>>
>>>
>>> The other issue is that of repeated matrix factorizations in the
>>> mdivide_left and log_determinant varis.  I'd like to create a single
>>> "factorization" vari which can be used to solve linear systems,
>>> compute determinants, etc and only ever factorize the matrix once.
>>> Before that though, I'd just like to avoid repeatedly factorizing a
>>> matrix at construction and in chain().  In principle this shouldn't be

>>> needed since the cleanup() function will probably empty 99% of the
>>> time.

>>> up, it is added to a special list which is traversed at cleanup time.

>>>

messages.subject: | is not a synonym for ||
messages.body_plain:
The single vbar (|) is for bitwise or.

The double vbar (||) is for logical or.

There are two reasons to use the logical-or operation
for logical operations:

  1.  it's clearer what the intent is, and

  2.  it works by short circuiting, so if the first
      disjunct is true, the whole thing evaluates to true
      without considering the other disjuncts.

- Bob

Regarding use case, I don't think the users understand the contract that you've described with using set_cppo("fast"). messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Testing Private/Protected Methods
messages.body_plain:
For protected methods, you need to write mock extensions
to test them.

You don't need to test private methods.  They're not part
of the public (or protected) API.  They're "implementation
details".  If you have independently testable functionality in private
methods, they should probably be made public or pulled out of
the class.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Binom_coeff_log in fvar broken after merge master
messages.body_plain:
On 4/10/13 6:59 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> When I merged master to the fvar branch to update includes to reflect the refactoring, I got an error for binom_coeff_log(const T1& x1, const fvar<T2>& x2). The code for in the fvar file is
>
>     template <typename T1, typename T2>
>     inline
>     fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>
>     binomial_coefficient_log(const T1& x1, const fvar<T2>& x2){
>       using boost::math::digamma;
>       using std::log;
>       using stan::math::binomial_coefficient_log;
>       const double cutoff = 1000;
>       if ((x1 < cutoff) || (x1 - x2.val_ < cutoff)) {

binomial_coefficient_log only technically makes sense for integers,
but we've generalized it by replacing the factorials with gamma
functions.

If we don't ever call this with negative values for x2,
then you only need the second test here.

>         return fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>(
>                    binomial_coefficient_log(x1, x2.val_),
>                    - x2.d_ * digamma(x2.val_ + 1)
>                    - x2.d_ * digamma(x1 - x2.val_ + 1));
>       } else {
>         return fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>(
>           binomial_coefficient_log(x1, x2.val_), x2.d_
>           * log(x1 - x2.val_) + (x2.val_ * (0 - x2.d_)) / (x1 - x2.val_))
>           + 0 * log(x1 / (x1 - x2.val_)) + (x1 + 0.5) / (x1 / (x1 - x2.val_))
>           * (0 * (x1 - x2.val_) - (0 - x2.d_) * x1) / ((x1 - x2.val_)
>           * (x1 - x2.val_)) + 0 / (12 * x1 * x1) - x2.d_ + (0 - x2.d_)
>           / (12 * (x1 - x2.val_) * (x1 - x2.val_)
>           - digamma(x2.val_ + 1) * x2.d_);
>       }

You should format these long statements into terms that can be more easily
digested.  For long sums, I use the following format:

          return fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>(
            binomial_coefficient_log(x1, x2.val_),
            x2.d_ * log(x1 - x2.val_)
              + (x2.val_ * (0 - x2.d_)) / (x1 - x2.val_))
              + 0 * log(x1 / (x1 - x2.val_))
              + (x1 + 0.5) / (x1 / (x1 - x2.val_))
                  * (0 * (x1 - x2.val_) - (0 - x2.d_) * x1) / ((x1 - x2.val_)
                  * (x1 - x2.val_))
              + 0 / (12 * x1 * x1)
              - x2.d_
              + (0 - x2.d_) / (12 * (x1 - x2.val_) * (x1 - x2.val_)
              - digamma(x2.val_ + 1) * x2.d_
            );
>     }
>
> The test code giving the error is
>
>   double w = 2006.0;
>   fvar<double> y(1002.0);
>   y.d_ = 2.0;
>
>   fvar<double> c = binomial_coefficient_log(w, y);

This is good that you're testing with a multiplier of 2.0
in y.d_.  It tests that we're not forgetting to multiply,
which is easy to do if the initial derivative is 1.0.

>   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(binomial_coefficient_log(2006.0, 1002.0), c.val_);
>   EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(2.0 * log(2006.0 - 1002.0) + (1002.0 * (0 - 2.0))
>                   / (2006.0 - 1002.0) + 0 * log(2006.0 / (2006.0 - 1002.0))
>                   + (2006.0 + 0.5) / (2006.0 / (2006.0 - 1002.0)) * (0
>                   * (2006.0 - 1002.0) - (0 - 2.0) * 2006.0) / ((2006.0 - 1002.0)
>                   * (2006.0 - 1002.0)) + 0 / (12 * 2006.0 * 2006.0) - 2.0
>                   + (0 - 2.0) / (12 * (2006.0 - 1002.0) * (2006.0 - 1002.0))
>                   - digamma(1002.0 + 1) * 2.0, c.d_);
>
> After testing, I found that there was nothing wrong with the binom_coeff_log fvar file, as I used print statements to print out the values that should've been stored as c.val_ and c.d_--these were correct.
>
> However, something is causing the wrong c.val_ and c.d_ to be returned--the returned values are the ones that should be returned if (x1 < cutoff) || (x1 - x2.val_ < cutoff). This is particularly confusing since when I added a print statement in the if loop to see if it was ever called, nothing was printed..

I'd go back and recheck these steps.  I don't have any better suggestion
than tracing.  You can try calling the fvar version of binomial_coefficient_log
directly.   If your function's not getting called, something else must be.
Are you sure you have the right include statements in place?

- Bob

messages.subject: Bug in init/data parsing
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

There appears to be a bug with how dump files are parsed when they're
passed as data or as init.  I've attached a simple test case which
demonstrates the problem.

The model has a data matrix and a parameter matrix which have the same
dimension and are given the same data/initialization values.  When run
the model produces the following:

$ ./datatest --point_estimate --iter=0 --data=datatest.data --init=datatest.data
STAN OPTIMIZATION COMMAND
data = datatest.data
init = datatest.data
output = samples.csv
save_warmup = 0
seed = 37934482 (randomly generated)
y_param = 1:0, y_data = 1
y_param = 3:0, y_data = 2
y_param = 5:0, y_data = 3
y_param = 2:0, y_data = 4
y_param = 4:0, y_data = 5
y_param = 6:0, y_data = 6
...

\It looks like the bug is in the handling of the inits as y_data is
parsed in column-major order as it shouild be but I haven't been able
to track it down.

Anyone willing to take a stab?  I've run out of time and ideas for the day.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
There's an Eigen-specific flag we should be using
to turn off their error bounds.  -DNDEBUG turns off
their bounds checking, too, but we can just turn off
their bounds checks.  (We don't need to use Eigen's
checks because we check everything before sending it
to Eigen.)

We'll get that into the next release.

- Bob

messages.subject: (R)Stan 1.3.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Stan 1.3.0 and RStan 1.3.0 are available for download.
Follow the links on:

    Stan home page:  http://mc-stan.org/

Please let us know if you have problems updating.

- Stan Development Team

v1.3.0 (12 April 2013)
======================================================================

Enhancements
----------------------------------
Modeling Language
* forward sampling (random draws from distributions)
   in generated quantities
* better error messages in parser
* additional distributions:
     + exp_mod_normal
     + gumbel
     + skew_normal
* additional functions:
     + owenst
* broadcast (repetition) functions for vectors, arrays, matrices
     + rep_arrray
     + rep_matrix
     + rep_row_vector
     + rep_vector

Command-Line
* added option to display autocorrelations in the command-line program
   to print output
* changed default point estimation routine from the command line to
   use Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, added option for point
   estimation with Newton's method

RStan
* added method as.mcmc.list()
* compatibility with R 3.0.0

C++/Internal
* refactored math/agrad libs in C++ to separate files/includes,
   remove redundant code, more unit tests for existing code
* added chainable_alloc class for caching solver results
* generalized VectorView with seq_view
* templated out generated code for efficient double-only operation
   on model log probs w/o gradients

Doc
* additions to user's guide w. sample models
     + stochastic volatility example with source, optimized source,
       simulation
     + time series, moving average, standardization for linear
       regression, hidden Markov models, with examples
* manual's index is now hyperlinked
* added additional acknowledgements to manual
* added full description of differences between sampling
   statement and lp__
* fixed general normal mixture model example

Testing
* split unit tests from distribution tests

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------
* fixed derivative in multi_normal_prec distribution function
* double-based log_prob functions return the same value as var-based
   log_prob_grad functions
* calls to lgamma are now using boost's lgamma function
* patched transform to work with Eigen 3.2 beta
* all probability distribution functions and cumulative distribution
   functions behave properly with 0 length vector arguments
* fixed error in definition of hypergeometric pmf
* fixed arguments to nesterov optimization ctor in command
* fixed issue with initialization matrices being read improperly
* Use fabs() instead of abs() in unit_vector_constrain.
* typos in the manual
* rstan:
   + fixed crash in R when index is out of bounds using set_cppo("fast")
   + io_context fix skipping len=0
   + fix the typo in manual (dims -> dim)
   + add require(inline) to fix the problem with loading sysdata.rda

messages.subject: Precompiled header confusion
messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to address a point about precompiled headers while it's still in my memory.

On Sat, Apr 13, 2013 at 5:57 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I was getting ready to run this tool again. But first I ran into an issue that confused me. I had thought that
>
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ find src/stan -name '*.hpp' -print | xargs -n 1 -P 7 clang++ -x c++-header -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2/ -I lib/boost_1.53.0/ -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS 2> /tmp/pch_errors.txt
>
> would succeed in making a precompiled header out of every .hpp file in stan/src/.

I also had the same misconception about precompiled headers. For any build, there can only be 1 (one) precompiled header. It has to be included first in the file and it only works under certain compilers. (I think it doesn't work for Windows g++ and Mac's clang++, but it does work for Mac g++.) I've made that mistake and built one for each header (which took hours) only to find out that's not how it works.

For our build, that single header is src/stan/model/model_header.hpp. That's why it has so much included int it. If after a build, you see a src/stan/model/model_header.hpp.pch or model_header.hpp.gch, you've got a precompiled header. The flags that control it in our build are in os_* and the variable is called PCH. The place it actually gets built is in make/models towards the end.

I haven't successfully gotten the build time down by using a precompiled header. The issue we have is the number of template instantiations going on, which can't be addressed with the precompiled header. What Bob's suggested in his 3/20 email titled "how much can we precompile? + privacy" is where we could actually make improvements to our build times. This is the section that's relevant:

On Wed, Mar 20, 2013 at 2:57 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
Topic I
-------

One issue that would be nice to address in this
refactoring is the time it takes to compile user models.

One thing we could do to speed this up is more
agressively precompile our libs.

The most general way to do this is to follow the
pattern set up in the grammars (which was forced
upon us by Windows compiler lameness).

The general idea is for each function foo()
would be to have three separate files:

   foo.hpp   pure header file, included by clients
             who link against the precompile lib

   foo_def.hpp   actual definitions, included by
                 clients who want to use Stan as
                 a header only lib

   foo_inst.cpp  instantiations of the function's templates,
                 compiled into an archive for users to link
                 against;  includes foo_def.hpp

Right now, the boundary between what gets separated
into .hpp and .cpp files seems rather arbitrary.

At this point, I'm all for splitting our build. I think we can engineer it so that it costs a bunch of time once to build out the instantiations that would be standard in a Stan build, and then every model would be relatively quick to compile. It would cost us some time to engineer it properly, but we can eat that cost. (By we, I mean I'm willing to volunteer if no one else steps up.)

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I found a bug in the new code.  It's a subtle one not likely to show
up on some systems, but I've seen it crash things in subtle and hard
to track down ways elsewhere so I thought I'd point it out.  Here is
the code from check_pos_definite.hpp

     std::ostringstream msg_o;
     msg_o << name << error_msg << error_msg2;
     T_result tmp =
raise_domain_error<T_result,T_y>(function,msg_o.str().c_str(),y,boost::math::policies::policy<>());

The issue is that msg_o.str().c_str() will produce a pointer to memory
which has been freed.  The str() method returns a new, temporary
instance of a std::string.  Once c_str() returns, that temporary
instance of the std::string will be destroyed, leaving the pointer
returned by c_str() pointing to a buffer which has just been deleted.

I'm not sure how widespread that pattern is, so I thought I'd email
rather than fix it in one or two places and have it persist elsewhere.

Cheers,
Marcus

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/TopicPreprocessorDirectives.html

which says:
EIGEN_DEFAULT_DENSE_INDEX_TYPE - the type for column and row indices in matrices, vectors and array (DenseBase::Index <http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1DenseBase.html#a4d4873e91be950c079f067fa97fd5c40>). Set to std::ptrdiff_t by default.

So, I was wrong about remembering it being a size_t, and it is still signed. My commit should be reverted, but I'm still not sure why it was failing before.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I was thinking of changing the type of error_msg passed into dom_err
to be a template parameter.  Right now it's a const char* so anyone
using dom_error will have the same issue and will need to create a
temporary string, which makes this error more tempting and therefore
more likely.  If you could pass in a std::string, it would be less
likely to happen with people calling dom_err.

In dom_err itself you'll still need to create the temporary
std::string to get the c_str() to pass to raise_domain_error.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Minor bug with initializations/bounded variables
messages.body_plain:
This is a strange one which may not have an obvious solution, if any.
I've attached a simple model to demonstrate the problem.

If you do:

inittest --init=inittest.init --point_estimate

you'll see that the initial value of x is actually 1e35, instead of 1.
 (The same thing, plus some noise, happens without the
point_estimate.)  The problem is that the range of the bound is too
large and double precision is not enough to handle values that close
to one end.  In a sense, there's nothing we can do here short of using
long doubles (which seems like definite overkill...)

There are two issues that I see here.

1) It would be nice to catch this kind of error with the
initialization and report it to the user.

2) If people unwittingly set really large bounds like this, the
sampling is likely to produce incorrect results if the posterior
probability is mostly located near one end of the bound or another due
to discretization.  This should definitely be mentioned in the manual
and it might even be worth trying to figure out what the "largest"
range is and print a warning if it comes up at run time.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: bug in inv_cloglog formula
messages.body_plain:
The formula for inv_cloglog is wrong.  It should be:

   inv_cloglog(y) =  1 - exp(-exp(y))

   cloglog(x) = log(-log(1 - x))

I'm going to fix that and also include cloglog
for the next release.

- Bob

messages.subject: LDLT Factorizations
messages.body_plain:
I'm about to push a bunch of changes which I will describe in a series
of emails.  The work, done over the past week or so, come together to
make Stan much faster in a number of ways (any models using multI_* or
*wishart distributions should be much faster), and in particular,
greatly improves the ability to work with Gaussian Process models.

Without further ado...

1) LDLT_factor

I've introduced an LDLT_factor<T> class and a set of functions which
use it, i.e., log_determinant_ldlt, mdivide_left_ldlt,
mdivide_right_ldlt.  This is a C++ only interface.

This class ensures that any function which uses the above operations
on a symmetric, positive definite matrix only ever needs to compute
the decomposition once, including to perform the positive-definiteness
check.  Now, as a rule, check_pos_definite should never be used unless
that is the *only* use.  If any of the above operations will be needed
on that matrix, use LDLT_factor instead.

I've gone through and updated the multi_gp_log, multi_normal_log,
multi_student_t_log, wishart_log and inv_wishart_log functions to make
use of it.  I'm not sure if there are any other potential targets or
not, feel free to let me know if I've missed anything.

This code is not the prettiest and will probably be cleaned up a bit
over time, and some more thorough error checking included.  In the
meantime let me know if you have any comments on the code or design.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Multivariate GPs
messages.body_plain:
I'm about to push a bunch of changes which I will describe in a series
of emails.  The work, done over the past week or so, come together to
make Stan much faster in a number of ways (any models using multI_* or
*wishart distributions should be much faster), and in particular,
greatly improves the ability to work with Gaussian Process models.

Next up we have...

2) Multivariate Gaussian Processes

I've added (actually completed to be precise) the multi_gp_log
function.  It is best explained with an example:

matrix[yDim,N] y; // matrix of outputs
matrix[N,N] K; // kernel matrix
vector[yDim] w; // individual scales for each output dimension

for (i in 1:yDim)
  row(y,i) ~ multi_normal(zeros,(1/w[i])*K));

With multi_gp_log, the above can be done much more efficiently and
compactly with:

y ~ multi_gp(K,w);

I've added some rudimentary tests, although they're probably not as
comprehensive they should be.  Currently there is no documentation.
If someone wants to expand the GP section of the manual to describe
this, that would be awesome.  Otherwise, it may take me a while to do
it.

2.5) GP Kernel computation

I've implemented a squared_dist function and vari, which makes
computing a squared exponential kernel more efficient.  Instead of:

K[i,j] <- exp(-alpha*dot_self(col(x,i) - col(x,j)));

you can write

K[i,j] <- exp(-alpha*squared_dist(col(x,i),col(x,j)));

which saves a fair amount of varis since this line would be executed
O(N^2) times.  I've implemented unit tests for the squared_dist
function, but no documentation yet.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: BFGS Optimization
messages.body_plain:
I'm about to push a bunch of changes which I will describe in a series
of emails.  The work, done over the past week or so, come together to
make Stan much faster in a number of ways (any models using multI_* or
*wishart distributions should be much faster), and in particular,
greatly improves the ability to work with Gaussian Process models.

Finally...

3) BFGS Implementation

When trying to optimize a GPLVM-type model I found the Nesterov method
to have poor convergence (it very quickly stopped making significant
progress) and the Newton method to be too slow due to the need for the
Hessian.  Instead I've implemented a BFGS-based quasi-Newton method
with line search (using the strong Wolfe conditions, for anyone
keeping score).  The implementation should be fairly robust and for
people looking to use point estimates (*ducking Andrews glare*) I
would recommend this be the default, first-try method.  Right now it
is available with --point_estimate_bfgs.

This is not quite the ideal optimizer in my mind, as it may become too
expensive for problems with more than ~20k parameters.  L-BFGS would
be better, but I doubt I'll get to implementing that in the near
future.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wednesday, April 17, 2013 1:54:40 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> I wouldn't object to someone adding an option to use the weak Wolfe
> conditions, but I'd need to read over that paper carefully before I'd
> suggest it as a default.

Perhaps I should have said that Overton's optimization software

http://www.cs.nyu.edu/overton/software/hanso/

uses weak Wolfe as a default, and I wasn't going to disagree with him.

I don't know of a case where weak Wolfe is insufficient for convergence, although you can get faster convergence on sufficiently well-behaved problems with strong Wolfe. But it is not too hard to construct a problem where strong Wolfe doesn't work numerically. So, that is the argument for a weak Wolfe default in a nutshell.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Matt and Andrew.

With the changes I've just pushed, I would think it should be very
plausible to fit a GP with a couple hundred data points using MCMC in
Stan in a reasonable period of time.

Right now I can fit (using MAP) a GP-based latent variable model with
~2k data points using BFGS in under 30min on a 3yr old Macbook Pro.
Fitting just hyperparameters for a GP regression/classification
problem should be even faster.

That said, the performance we have right now is pretty close to
optimal for Stan for most typical GP models.  There are a couple
places we could make it even faster, but I suspect they would only
shave off maybe 10% or 15% of runtime.

Cheers,
Marcus

You want to do it for all types T,
but you still want to return what
numeric_limits<double> returns.

All the types T you'll implement it for
will have implicit constructors T(double)
that will build the appropriate type out
of doubles.

At the very least, we'll need the following
for RM-HMC in Stan:

   fvar<double>
   fvar<var>
   fvar<fvar<double>>
   fvar<fvar<var>>

But they can all be implemented with one template.
And templating will also let client code plug in
float instead of double or some other base scalar
type.

- Bob

I've implemented a lot of fvar/matrix (and it's all tested and in master already)--only 29.7 Linear Algebra Functions and Solvers left.

I've run into a few things:

It looks like a premature typedef in typedefs.hpp.  I
think it should be this:

     typedef Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>::Index size_type;

instead of

     typedef typename internal::traits<Derived>::size_type size_type;

I think the intention was to have EigenDenseBaseAddons.hpp loaded
first, which I think adds a size_type static variable for matrices.
If that gets loaded first the original typedef would work.  But
the one with Index should work eithe way.

Daniel added this flexiblity to allow us to write polymorphic code across
Eigen data structures and std::vector.

I'm running unit tests to confirm that fixing the typedef
doesn't break anything, and it'll hopefully fix your compile problem.
If it persists, we probably have to figure out how to reorder
some more global includes.

I'd prefer to just get rid of the typedef in the stan::math
namespace altogether and be more explicit in uses.

Daniel and I will get together and settle on a standard way
to approach types.  The up-and-coming Eigen 3.2 lets you configure
the index type directly, which would let us just standardize
on size_t for indexing everything.

- Bob

On Friday, April 19, 2013 4:16:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Daniel and I will get together and settle on a standard way
> to approach types.  The up-and-coming Eigen 3.2 lets you configure
> the index type directly, which would let us just standardize
> on size_t for indexing everything.

It has been configurable for dense matrices since 3.0. But the Eigen people had a long discussion about this and decided that signed types were better, mostly due to avoiding bugs in loops. I don't think there are too many cases in statistical modeling where one wants a matrix whose rows or columns is more than a signed integer can hold. So, I'm not convinced that standardizing on size_t would be a good thing.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stepsize Jitter Back
messages.body_plain:
We should leave those there until we want to
break backward compatibility.

Then we can expose more if anyone wants to.

Marcus had a good idea as to redefining syntax,
which is to have defaults with structure:

   stan sample [general sampler args]
   stan optimize [general optimizer args]

and then specific subcommands for users who want to
control the sampler parameters

   stan hmc [hmc args] [general sampler args]
   stan metropolis [metropolis args] [general sampler args]
   ...

   stan bfgs [bfgs args] [general optimizer args]
   ...

BUT, we don't want to do this until Stan 2.0.0 if
it's at all possible to keep things backward
compatible for the next release.

IF we can sort out good options for all of this now,
then we could push up 2.0.0 to whenever the new
versions are completed.

Then 2.1.0 or 3.0.0 can be the RM-HMC release.  Then people
will really be on our case about version creep!

- Bob

Is there an equivalent of std::endl for carriage return?

It used to overwrite, but then I went back to just writing
out one at a time due to portability issues.

Right now, we have std::endl in command-line code,
which generates platform-specific output.  But we
have "\n" hard-coded into the code generator and
into our output file generation to standardize on
unix-style newlines.

messages.body_plain:
> I realize it's now a diagonal mass matrix instead
> of varying step sizes (I'll have to change the manual
> to reflect that).

Yes, when switching to a proper metric instead of the "varying step sizes" the step-size and metric elements became identifiable and so the adaptation had to be factored.  Basically the variance (or covariance for dense) is estimated using the Welford algorithm while the step-size is estimated using dual-averaging.

> But did the estimation strategy change so the dual
> averaging params are no longer relevant?  If so, it
> doesn't make sense to leave them in place.

No, they're used but take default values from internal constructors.  It was just odd that we exposed two of the dual-averaging parameters but not the others, so I ignored the option to set them by hand when refactoring.  I'd rather we make them all available, which the subcommands would make easy.  For now I'll de-neuter the two existing options on master.

>
> And it won't really be "stan" from the command line,
> but "my_model sample".
>
> The executable is just "my_model", as now, but the first
> thing it'll do is look at what the next argument is,
> which would be required to be one of the subcommands.
> That is, it should work like subcommands in git or svn.
>
> It'd also be nice to have it check options, so that
> unrecognized options are rejected.

Yup, exactly what I was thinking.  But how exactly do we implement it?  Right now stan::io::cmd_line is agnostic to the commands, it just accumulates them and allows the user to query but any subcommand functionality would either require listing all of the possible command/subcommand relationships in stan::io::cmd_line or changing the syntax of the arguments.  For example,

1)  Denote subcommands with a prefix, such as s_

my_model sample hmc s_hmc_arg1 s_hmc_arg2 da s_da_arg1

This way, as stan::io::cmd_line reads the arguments it can associate commands (unprefixed) with subcommands (everything with the prefix immediately following the unprefixed command).  But it's really ugly.

2) Denote subcommands with equals

my_model sample hmc:hmc_arg1,hmc_arg2 da:da_arg1

Again, easy to parse without knowing the command/subcommand relationships.  Less ugly, but still pretty ugly.

3)  Denote commands as flags

my_model sample -hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 -da da_arg1

4) Lookup table after parsing:

my_model sample hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 da da_arg1

gets parsed to a list

args=[hmc, hmc_arg1, hmc_arg2, da, da_arg1]

Then you just run over the list checking against a look-up table of commands and their subcommands.

5)  Lookup table before parsing:

my_model sample hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 da da_arg1

While parsing you check against the big look-up table (which would have to be stored in stan::io::cmd_line now, unless we make a big giant class just to store the info).  This way you can also restrict valid subcommands to those immediately following the command.

I'm just not sure what everyone's preference is. 3 seems to be the standard SVN approach although 5 wouldn't be that hard.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
messages.body_plain:
I'm fine with whatever adaptation strategy works best. But we should
really have a way of determining that before making changes to core
functionality.

Also, I don't think the choice between multiple step sizes/diagonal
mass matrices in any way affects the identifiability question. The
position and energy trajectories are *in no way* changed by that
implementation choice. Any identifiability issues associated with one
implementation are every bit as present in the other; even if they're
obscured, they'll still affect the speed with which the adaptation
converges.

I do think it's important to factorize the questions of overall and
relative step size estimation, which means scaling the mass matrix so
that something (largest eigenvalue? smallest eigenvalue? trace?) is
constant.

Also, I think that even with the current strategy we're much too
sensitive to the early iterations when fitting the per-variable step
sizes. Estimates of the covariance matrix from the initial warmup
samples are garbage—they only tell you how far away you initialized
the sampler from a mode. I'd like to have the mass matrix adaptation
turned off until we have some reason to believe that things have kind
of stabilized.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
messages.body_plain:
> Also, I don't think the choice between multiple step sizes/diagonal
> mass matrices in any way affects the identifiability question. The
> position and energy trajectories are *in no way* changed by that
> implementation choice. Any identifiability issues associated with one
> implementation are every bit as present in the other; even if they're

> converges.
>
> I do think it's important to factorize the questions of overall and
> relative step size estimation, which means scaling the mass matrix so
> that something (largest eigenvalue? smallest eigenvalue? trace?) is
> constant.

This is not exactly true.  The problem is that, in general, you can't scale the metric arbitrarily; only in the specific case of the explicit leapfrog integrator do you have that freedom.  In that case you can perform a symplectomorphism

P = (L^{T})^{-1} p
Q = L^{-1} q

and then write the integrator in terms of P and q so that you always have (epsilon * (L^{T})^{-1}) grouped together, and you're free to exchange scales arbitrarily.  Because the refactoring was meant to separate the sampling algorithm, the Hamiltonian, the integrator, and the potential such a strategy was not feasible.  In particular, it wouldn't work for RMHMC and implementing it would require an architecture necessitating rewrites for each new algorithm.

That said, the only real difference in the adaptation is that an update in the metric now necessitates a corresponding update of the step size or else the acceptance rate will be off.  Given the performance of your step size initialization routine,  however, that's hardly a problem.

> Also, I think that even with the current strategy we're much too
> sensitive to the early iterations when fitting the per-variable step
> sizes. Estimates of the covariance matrix from the initial warmup
> samples are garbage—they only tell you how far away you initialized
> the sampler from a mode. I'd like to have the mass matrix adaptation
> turned off until we have some reason to believe that things have kind
> of stabilized.

Agreed.  Implementing a better warm-up is on my very long, and rapidly growing, to-do list.  Hopefully once I'm settled I'll be able to burn through a bunch of it quickly and get to the warm-up sooner rather than later.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
messages.body_plain:
I think stan::prob makes more sense than stan::math.

I'd rather not introduce multiple inheritance of
implementations if we don't have to.

I'd much rather see you just include an instance
(not a reference to an instance) as a member variable.

As a design strategy, containing is much more flexible
than inheriting because you can choose what to expose.
It does mean you need to define the
methods again where you just need to pass-through
results from the accumulator.  But you probably want
to name them something different anyway.

If you do multistage warmups, you probably do NOT
want to call init() twice.  Or you should at least
name it something other than init().  Maybe an
init() to do allocation, etc. and a reset()?
Then init() can call reset()?

With lots of structures in programs, it's much easier
to reason about them if they get constructed once.
It's not that expensive to construct a new object
and a lot cleaner than tweaking an existing one.
The tweak needs to be sure to clear all the state,
and if done incrementally, to insure consistency.

- Bob

optimization (but then it'll be slower to run).  You might
also try squeezing it in using the clang++ compiler.

messages.body_plain:
Jon had installed rstan on the hotfoot before. I guess the version of gcc is still less than 4.2.1.  You can see the version of gcc by executing 'gcc -v', which might be helpful to identify the problem.

But there is a gcc44 installed on hotfoot, which is not the default one.  So in Stan, you need to add "CC=g++44" after "make bin/stanc".

For R, you need to create, in your home directory, a new directory (unless it already exists):

mkdir .R

and then within this new directory, with your favorite editor, create a file named "Makevars", containing the following two lines.

CXX = g++44
SHLIB_CXXLD = g++44

--
Jiqiang

> Or it might be possible to compile a binary
> somewhere else that you can use on the cluster -- Ben or someone
> involved in the cluster might know how to do that or if it'd

The default g++ on Hotfoot is 4.1.2 which is not known to have ever worked (in addition to the possible memory problems). So, you need to explicitly specify g++4.4 on the command line to have a fighting chance. Or if trying to install RStan, you need a file in $HOME/.R/Makevars that contains at least these lines

CC=gcc44
CXX=g++44

I doubt the cluster is binary compatible with anything I have, but dropping a binary in might be possible in principle.

Ben

On Apr 22, 2013, at 2:18 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I think stan::prob makes more sense than stan::math.
>
> I'd rather not introduce multiple inheritance of
> implementations if we don't have to.
>
> I'd much rather see you just include an instance
> (not a reference to an instance) as a member variable.
>
> As a design strategy, containing is much more flexible
> than inheriting because you can choose what to expose.
> It does mean you need to define the
> methods again where you just need to pass-through
> results from the accumulator.  But you probably want
> to name them something different anyway.

Oh, I was referring to multiple inheritance in the adaptive samplers.  For example

class adapt_diag_e_nuts: public diag_e_nuts, public stepsize_adapter, public var_adapter

so that var_adapter doesn't have to inherent from stepsize_adapter unnecessarily.  var_adapter would hold the instance of welford_var_estimator

> If you do multistage warmups, you probably do NOT
> want to call init() twice.  Or you should at least
> name it something other than init().  Maybe an
> init() to do allocation, etc. and a reset()?
> Then init() can call reset()?
>
> With lots of structures in programs, it's much easier
> to reason about them if they get constructed once.
> It's not that expensive to construct a new object
> and a lot cleaner than tweaking an existing one.

messages.body_plain:
Two issues.

1.  What should the unconstrained param names be?

They're not in 1-1 correspondence with

   type          constrained    unconstrained
   simplex           K               K-1
   corr_matrix      K*K             (K choose 2)
   cov_matrix       K*K             K + (K choose 2)

corr_matrix (K choose 2 vs. K*K), cov_matrix (K + K choose 2
vs. K*K).  [I'm guessing the unit-length normed variables behave
like simplex, but I haven't looked that closely.]

Can I just dump out the name and then the index in the
unconstrained vector?  So every name would be either
"foo" or "foo.<N>", where <N> is the param index (indexing
from 1, of course).

2.  There's an issue with how things are currently organized
that's making it hard for me to give Michael the method he
wants:

   -  void get_constrained_values(vector<double>& v, const vector<double>& r, const vector<int>& i)

The problem is that the unconstrained parameters r aren't quite
enough to generate all the output values because there's potentially
RNG involved in the generated quantities block.   I had assumed
that the write method would just be called once and in so
doing generates the random quantities.

There's currently a method on models that does what you want:

     template <typename RNG>
     void write_array(RNG& base_rng__,                                // in
                      std::vector<double>& params_r_constrained__,    // in
                      std::vector<int>& params_i__,                   // in
                      std::vector<double>& params_r_unconstrained__,  // out
                      std::ostream* pstream__ = 0);                   // out (optional)

KEY:

   v == vars__
   r == params_r__
   i == params_i__

The RNG base_rng__ is used to generate the random quantities that
might be needed in generated quantities.  Are you OK passing
an RNG in?

Also, passing the pstream in for error reporting?

After the above method is called, the params_r_unconstrained__ vector
will contain the values of parameters, transformed parameters, and
generated quantities, in the same order as they are printed.

We can rename this method to be consistent.

The write_csv method is similar, but writes directly to a CSV
file instead of populating an array.  I'm eventually going to change
the implementation of write_csv to collect up an array by calling
write_array (or get_constrained_values) and then printing what
comes out to the print stream.

- Bob

messages.subject: kronecker products
messages.body_plain:
On 4/25/13 1:03 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
>
>     The distribution indeed requires the Kronecker product, so I've followed Ben's suggestion and programmed it element
>     by element. It's not fast, but will have to do for the time being ;) Thank you for taking a look!
>
>
> Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little bit by
> being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)
>
> |
> t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y
> |
>
> you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W. Particularly
> if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.
>
> This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance
> improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.

We're still working on the refactor.  After that happens,
we'll be in much better shape to add new data types.

We'll have the same problem (though not as extreme)
right now if we try to implement Cholesky factors.
Specifically, we'd need to get the triangular views in
the right places.  One way to do that in the current setup
(that is, without changing the way the code's generated
very much) would be to have functions that were defined
specifically on triangular views like some of our functions
do now.  It's clunky and we wouldn't want to replicate
all of our matrix functions for triangular views, but it
might let us squeeze out most of the performance we want.

It looks like there's an unsupported module in Eigen for
Kronecker products, but I was expecting an expression template,
not a dense product:

https://bitbucket.org/eigen/eigen/src/0cf501b7d3dd/unsupported/Eigen/src/KroneckerProduct/KroneckerTensorProduct.h

Am I reading that correctly?  Line 51 looks like a killer:

AB.block(i*Br,j*Bc,Br,Bc) = A(i,j)*B;

This we could do in Stan with a function

     kronecker_multiply(A,B)

and we could make the auto-diff much more efficient, but it's
still going to be a space hog.

What do people do with kronecker products once they create them?
Can we attack the problem one level up?  Is one of the terms
here going to be a kronecker product?

 > t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y

That's the kind of op we could wrap up.

- Bob

messages.subject: command options & adaptation for Metropolis
messages.body_plain:
Peter's got the basic Metropolis working end to end, so
it's time to think about adaptation and configuration.

1.  How do we want Metropolis to be configurable?
     At very least, I'm imagining:

        -- adapted single step size * unit covariance

        -- adapted diagonal covariance matrix

        -- adapted full covariance matrix

Do we need to include user-specified step sizes and user-specified
covar matrices in addition?

If so, any suggestions on how to set up the classes?
Specifically, do we have three classes,

    metropolis_unit_covar
    metropolis_diag_covar
    metropolis_full_covar

that let us configure adaptation vs. user input, or six
classes, the above plus user-specified matrix versions?

2.  How should we be doing adaptation for Metropolis?

Does it make sense to independently adapt a global
scale (step size in HMC) and a standardized
covariance matrix (inverse mass matrix in HMC)?
We can't just let both be free due to identifiability
issues, right?

Here's what I'm imagining:

   - parameters: scale epsilon, standardized covariance Sigma_std;
     proposal covariance matrix:  Sigma = epsilon * Sigma_std

   - initialize covariance matrix Sigma to unit diagonal

   - find a scale epsilon that gives us roughly 23.4% acceptance rates
     [or make acceptance rate target configurable]

   - run warmup iterations after 100 (200, 400, ...) iterations:
       + use last half of iterations' acceptance rate to adjust
         epsilon up or down
       + use last half of iterations to estimate standardized
         covariance matrix (???)

How do we standardize the covariance matrix estimate?

- Bob

version which estimates a covariance matrix given the previous samples
(full, diagonal or scaled identity) and then uses a mixture proposal
which uses the rescaled (see
http://probability.ca/jeff/ftpdir/galinart.pdf) estimated covariance
most of the time and sometimes uses a conservative proposal to avoid
excess sticking would be good.  Other possibilities are to use a
mixtures of multivariate Student T distributions which takes into

adapted covariance, whether to use student t or gaussian proposals,
etc.

thing, so no, I don't think it really makes sense to adapt a global

I was picturing a complete analogy to the HMC code,

metro_unit_covar
metro_diag_covar
metro_dense_covar

and then use multiple inheritance with the above and the adaptive sampler to yield

adapt_metro_unit_covar
adapt_metro_diag_covar
adapt_metro_dense_covar

> 2.  How should we be doing adaptation for Metropolis?
>
> Does it make sense to independently adapt a global
> scale (step size in HMC) and a standardized
> covariance matrix (inverse mass matrix in HMC)?
> We can't just let both be free due to identifiability
> issues, right?
>
> Here's what I'm imagining:
>
>  - parameters: scale epsilon, standardized covariance Sigma_std;
>    proposal covariance matrix:  Sigma = epsilon * Sigma_std
>
>  - initialize covariance matrix Sigma to unit diagonal
>
>  - find a scale epsilon that gives us roughly 23.4% acceptance rates
>    [or make acceptance rate target configurable]
>
>  - run warmup iterations after 100 (200, 400, ...) iterations:
>      + use last half of iterations' acceptance rate to adjust
>        epsilon up or down
>      + use last half of iterations to estimate standardized
>        covariance matrix (???)
>
> How do we standardize the covariance matrix estimate?

I don't think there will be identifiability issues here.  You have d(d -1) / 2 correlations for estimating the covariance and the Metropolis acceptance rate for estimating the step size.  Remember that the optimal scaling in Metropolis is not the covariance but some scaling of the covariance that depends on dimension (at least in IID gaussian models, etc).  Having a free step size will avoid our having to determine that a priori.

Again, I think we can reuse all the HMC code (which is why the reusable parts are in mcmc and not mcmc/hmc!).

1) Initialize covariance matrix to unit diagonal - the regularized estimator takes care of this for us.

2) Initialize stepsize to about 0.234 - 0.5 should be close enough for an initial guess.  Which means we can copy the init_stepsize code in HMC only using propose instead of evolve.

3) We should be able to adapt the step size as we go and then update the covariance after the usual windows.

 > Again, I think we can reuse all the HMC code (which is why the r

Sounds good.  Reuse base code for MCMC in both HMC and in Metropolis
and whatever else we do.

OK.

 > 2) Initialize stepsize to about 0.234 - 0.5 should be close enough for an initial guess.
 > Which means we can copy the init_stepsize code in HMC only using propose instead of evolve.

Why do we have to use init_stepsize() code in HMC if
we're just initializing to a fixed value?

And shouldn't that code go in stan::mcmc if we're going
to reuse it in Metropolis?   Or did you just mean
cut-and-paste it with modifications?

We used to have a find_reasonable_stepsize() method that
Matt wrote in the constructor for HMC/NUTS that tried to
find a step size with a decent acceptance rate before
starting.  Is this what init_stepsize() does?  And if so,
why does it keep getting called during adaptation?

 > 3) We should be able to adapt the step size as we go and then update the covariance after the usual windows.

How do we adapt the step size as we go?  It looks like what
it's doing now is calling the equivalent of find_reasonable_stepsize()
at each iteration, which multiplies step size by 2 or cuts it
in half repeatedly based on proposals (from an initial position or
what -- here's where the code loses me?).

(Aside question:  wouldn't a finer-grained factor like
like sqrt(2) or sqrt(sqrt(2)) be better?  Adaptation is slower
by a factor of 2 or 4,  but we'd get closer
than to within a factor of 2 of the "right" answer.)

I think I understand the covar matrix estimation, but let
me make sure.  At intervals during warmup (say after 100,
after 200, after 400 iterations, etc.), we'll take the
second half of the iterations (so after 100, we'd take
iterations 51--100, after 200 we take iterations 101-200) and
use the "sampled" parameter values to estimate a covariance matrix.
We can do this in a fixed amount of memory and reasonable numerical
stability with Welford's algorithm.

Until we get to the end.  If someone specifieds 875 warmup
iterations, then what do we do?  We'll have buffered
400--800, then we'll start again, but don't just want to use
the last 75.  And this'll be a huge mess in the time-based
approach when we don't even know how many warmup iterations
we'll get.

Also, someone mentioned only using the warmup iterations that
were not Metropolis rejected.  Should we do that?

- Bob

On 4/25/13 2:47 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, April 25, 2013 1:41:16 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     On 4/25/13 1:03 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>      > On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
>      >
>      >     The distribution indeed requires the Kronecker product, so I've followed Ben's suggestion and programmed it
>     element
>      >     by element. It's not fast, but will have to do for the time being ;) Thank you for taking a look!
>      >
>      >
>      > Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little
>     bit by
>      > being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)
>      >
>      > |
>      > t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y
>      > |
>      >
>      > you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W.
>     Particularly
>      > if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.
>      >
>      > This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance
>      > improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.
>
>     We're still working on the refactor.  After that happens,
>     we'll be in much better shape to add new data types.
>
>     We'll have the same problem (though not as extreme)
>     right now if we try to implement Cholesky factors.
>     Specifically, we'd need to get the triangular views in
>     the right places.  One way to do that in the current setup
>     (that is, without changing the way the code's generated
>     very much) would be to have functions that were defined
>     specifically on triangular views like some of our functions
>     do now.  It's clunky and we wouldn't want to replicate
>     all of our matrix functions for triangular views, but it
>     might let us squeeze out most of the performance we want.
>
>
> That is an issue but as long as the operations are not utilizing the upper triangular elements, then the waste is just
> allocating unnecessary zeros, which is small compared to the amount of waste involved in multiplying the Cholesky
> factors together and then Cholesky factorizing the product.

It's not the allocation of zeroes I'm worried about.
We can even use copies of the same stan::agrad::var
instance for that.  It's that if you then multiply them
without triangular views, you do a ton of extra work in
both the multiplication and in auto-dif of constant zeroes
(which our code won't be clever enough to figure out are
constant zeroes we don't care about).  But then putting back
in triangular views would take care of that issue.

I was thinking we either have special triangular-view functions,
or we somehow instrument the generated code so that every use
of a cholesky factor type is automatically wrapped in a triangular
view.

>     It looks like there's an unsupported module in Eigen for
>     Kronecker products, but I was expecting an expression template,
>     not a dense product:
>
>     https://bitbucket.org/eigen/eigen/src/0cf501b7d3dd/unsupported/Eigen/src/KroneckerProduct/KroneckerTensorProduct.h
>     <https://bitbucket.org/eigen/eigen/src/0cf501b7d3dd/unsupported/Eigen/src/KroneckerProduct/KroneckerTensorProduct.h>
>
>     Am I reading that correctly?  Line 51 looks like a killer:
>
>     AB.block(i*Br,j*Bc,Br,Bc) = A(i,j)*B;
>
>
> My understanding is that the Kronecker module in the unsupported/ part of Eigen would be inefficient for a variety of
> reasons in Stan.

And in Eigen!

>     This we could do in Stan with a function
>
>           kronecker_multiply(A,B)
>
>     and we could make the auto-diff much more efficient, but it's
>     still going to be a space hog.
>
>     What do people do with kronecker products once they create them?
>
>
> In statistical applications, the A and B are usually covariance matrices (and so is the result), and then used in
> multivariate densities and whatnot. The result is often sparse (even if represented as a dense Eigen::Matrix<>) and
> often multiplied from the left and the right by the same matrix. Also, they are often used in conjunction with the vec()
> operator, which is easy but not implemented in Stan yet.
>
> I started to mock up a class for this a few months ago whose unwritten methods could specialize the algebra of Kronecker
> products
>
> |
> template<typename T_A, typename T_B>
> class Kronecker {
> // see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_product
>      typedef typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T_covar,T_other>::type OutType;
>
> public:
>    const Kronecker(const Matrix<T_A,Dynamic,Dynamic> &,
>                    const Matrix<T_B,Dynamic,Dynamic> &);
>    const Kronecker(const Matrix<T_A,Dynamic,Dynamic> &);
>    const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_AoxB();
>    const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_A();
>    const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_B();
>    const Kronecker transpose();
>    const Kronecker inverse();
>    // specialize det(AoxB), eigenvalues(AoxB), singular_values(AoxB), and trace(AoxB)
>    const size_t rows() const;
>    const size_t cols() const;
>    const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const Kronecker &);
>    const Kronecker operator* (const double, const Kronecker &);
>    const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const double);
>    const Kronecker operator* (const var, const Kronecker &);
>    const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const var);
>    const EigenBase<Derived> operator* (const Kronecker &, const EigenBase<Derived> &);
>    const EigenBase<Derived> operator* (const EigenBase<Derived> &, const Kronecker &);
>    const EigenBase<Derived> operator/ (const EigenBase<Derived> &, const Kronecker &);
> protected:
>    EigenBase<Derived> m_A;
>    EigenBase<Derived> m_B;
> };

Right!  This is what you'd need to do for the efficient
expression template implementation in Eigen itself.  As is,
they're just giving you shorthand for a big matri that
gets allocated and filled.

Maybe it makes sense writing that and contributing it
to Eigen.  Not that it'd immediately help us in Stan.

The only other thing you'd need is operator()(int,int) and
operator()(int) [or whatever the right type is for indices].

>
>     Can we attack the problem one level up?  Is one of the terms
>     here going to be a kronecker product?
>
>       > t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y
>
>     That's the kind of op we could wrap up.
>

I think that's where the motivation would come from in Stan.
