On Apr 25, 2013, at 5:59 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

>> Why do we have to use init_stepsize() code in HMC if
>> we're just initializing to a fixed value?
>>
>> And shouldn't that code go in stan::mcmc if we're going
>> to reuse it in Metropolis?   Or did you just mean
>> cut-and-paste it with modifications?
>
>> We used to have a find_reasonable_stepsize() method that
>> Matt wrote in the constructor for HMC/NUTS that tried to
>> find a step size with a decent acceptance rate before
>> starting.  Is this what init_stepsize() does?  And if so,
>> why does it keep getting called during adaptation?
>
> I meant copy and paste with modifications.  The version in base_hmc is just Matt's algorithm tweaked slightly to use the proper (q, p) acceptance probability instead of just a (q) acceptance probability (which is really undefined since it's missing a volume correction).
>
>>> 3) We should be able to adapt the step size as we go and then update the covariance after the usual windows.
>>
>> How do we adapt the step size as we go?  It looks like what
>> it's doing now is calling the equivalent of find_reasonable_stepsize()
>> at each iteration, which multiplies step size by 2 or cuts it
>> in half repeatedly based on proposals (from an initial position or
>> what -- here's where the code loses me?).
>
> Init_stepsize is called only after --the (co)variance is updated--, not at every iteration.  The problem is that when you update the (co)variance the optimal step size changes, and initializing the step size again avoids unnecessary burden on the dual-averaging (remember we're not using a "standardized" metric anymore).
>
>> (Aside question:  wouldn't a finer-grained factor like
>> like sqrt(2) or sqrt(sqrt(2)) be better?  Adaptation is slower
>> by a factor of 2 or 4,  but we'd get closer
>> than to within a factor of 2 of the "right" answer.)
>
> Sure, I didn't consider any improvements but that would be easy.
>
>> I think I understand the covar matrix estimation, but let
>> me make sure.  At intervals during warmup (say after 100,
>> after 200, after 400 iterations, etc.), we'll take the
>> second half of the iterations (so after 100, we'd take
>> iterations 51--100, after 200 we take iterations 101-200) and
>> use the "sampled" parameter values to estimate a covariance matrix.
>> We can do this in a fixed amount of memory and reasonable numerical
>> stability with Welford's algorithm.
>
> Yes.
>
>> Until we get to the end.  If someone specifieds 875 warmup
>> iterations, then what do we do?  We'll have buffered
>> 400--800, then we'll start again, but don't just want to use
>> the last 75.  And this'll be a huge mess in the time-based
>> approach when we don't even know how many warmup iterations
>> we'll get.
>
> Yeah.  In fact, I think I've seen behavior to this effect already (it shows up as unoptimal acceptance rates in the final samples).
> Should we not make the windows arbitrary but scale them to the total number of warm-up iterations?  i.e. assume five windows and just take the first window to be of size (warm-up iterations) / 2^{5}, second window (warm-up) iterations) / 2^{4}, etc.
>
>> Also, someone mentioned only using the warmup iterations that
>> were not Metropolis rejected.  Should we do that?
>
> Only concern would be getting stuck in local minima.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command options & adaptation for Metropolis
messages.body_plain:
It also works for me.

Firstly, watch out out for the camelCase -- Bob's going to find you!  Move to prop_covar, etc.

Secondly, you've got some nastiness in your constructors

      adapt_dense_metro(M &m, BaseRNG& rng, std::ostream* error_msg)
        : dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg),
          stepsize_covar_adapter(m.num_params_r())
      {
        this->_propCov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
        this->_propCov.setIdentity();
      };

When the dense_metro constructor is called this->_propCov hasn't been constructed yet: you have a circular constructor!  Personally I wouldn't even pass var/covar as an argument (the Welford adaptation is pretty quick) but just a dimension to be used for constructing _propCov, especially if you're going to hide the option in the adapt_ classes!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command options & adaptation for Metropolis
messages.body_plain:
I was.

Here's the issue in detail.  You've defined the constructor as

    adapt_dense_metro(M &m, BaseRNG& rng, std::ostream* error_msg)
      : dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg),
        stepsize_covar_adapter(m.num_params_r())
    {
      this->_propCov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
      this->_propCov.setIdentity();
    };

When you try to construct adapt_dense_metro multiple constructors are called, from base to derived.  So in this case you call

base_mcmc()
base_metro()

dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg)

base_adapter()
stepsize_covar_adapter(m.num_params_r())

and then finally

    {
      this->_propCov.resize(m.num_params_r(), m.num_params_r());
      this->_propCov.setIdentity();
    };

Let's focus on the dense_metro constructor,

dense_metro<M, BaseRNG>(m, rng, this->_propCov, error_msg)

You've given this->_propCov as an argument, but it doesn't exist yet!  It only gets created once the arguments have been passed and the constructor executes.  It's like writing

double x = x;

I'm not sure what the spec says, but I wouldn't be surprised if it gives undefined behavior which would explain why Ben and I see different results than you.

-Mike

a simple test case is enough.  I'm wondering where the
non-positive def matrix came from (data, transformed data,

Yajuan:  this diagnostic you need to pay attention to:

 > Warning: integer division implicitly rounds to integer. Found int division: get_base1(vec_n,j,"vec_n",1) / N

You had "vec_n[j] / N" somewhere and both vec_n[j] and N are
integers.  Integer arithmetic rounds, e.g.,  1/3 = 0, 7/2 = 3, etc.
which is probably not what you want.

messages.subject: Memory leak in prob_agrad_ad::grad_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

Just an FYI that I've fixed a bug which manifested in memory-leak like
behaviour when exceptions were thrown.  Not sure if this is relevant
elsewhere but it's worth keeping an eye out for.

Basically, memory wouldn't get recovered and the arena allocator would
continue to grow when the log_prob function throws an exception.  The
fix is relatively simple: catch the exception, clear the memory and
rethrow the exception.

Also, I've added sub_row and sub_col functions which are basically
like the block() function but which return row/column vectors instead
of matrices.

Cheers,
Marcus

 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.

append_samples = 0
save_warmup = 0

To be precise, any extra samples wouldn't have affected anything because the (co)variance is updated only when a window closes, not when it opens.  In any case, I updated the adapters to take in the total number of adaptation iterations (just the number of warm up samples in our case) and then snap the final adaptation window to the total warmup window so that no samples are wasted.

It should be straightforward to make this work with time-based approaches, as well, if we can assume constant samples/time.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command options & adaptation for Metropolis
messages.body_plain:
The idea would be to estimate samples/time in vivo.  So instead of sampling until you hit the max time, like

sample
if(time > max_time) break

you would time each sample, use that to estimate the number of samples remaining in the given time window, and then set the total number of samples to equal to the samples already run plus those estimated to be remaining.

start clock
sample
stop clock
sample_per_time = (n * sample_per_time + 1 / (delta t) ) / ( n + 1)
samples_remaining = remaining_time * sample_per_time
n_samples = n + samples_remaining

The final timing would be less accurate, but you get to have both features.  There might be easier ways to accomplish this.

messages.body_plain:
What's the issue with not knowing number of
warmup iterations?

It'd be nice to have time per iteration estimators
even for the fixed number of iterations so we
can estimate time remaining.   I think it'd be nice
to be able to see iteration number, percentage
iterations complete, log probability, and
estimated time remaining.

As far as estimating time per iteration,
it might vary pretty widely during warmup, so
I'm not sure how stable it will be and when we
can do this.  Especially in the regime Andrew
imagines where you intentially start out at a point
that's likely to be too little time to converge.

Even after convergence, there can be a lot of
variation in tree depth explored (and hence time
taken per iteration).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Error Stream
messages.body_plain:
On 4/28/13 12:52 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I just want to confirm the new format for error handling.
 > Have all exceptions been removed in lieu of adding an error stream,
> or is the error stream in addition to the exceptions?

 > In particular, I'm thinking about how to call model::grad_log_prob properly.

The error handling in C++ now has a global configuration.
You can configure error handling to return NaN or
to throw exceptions (among other things).

We've configured the Stan modeling language to throw
exceptions.

The way we've dealt with calls to grad_log_prob is to
catch exceptions, print their messages to the error
stream, then treat it as a -infinity log probability.
NaN should be treated the same way (you can still get
NaN returns from std lib calls and some of our own that
we haven't added error checking policies to).

This combination of exceptions plus catch around calls
to log_prob lets us get an informative message
back to the user while still rejecting the parameter
state.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> What's the issue with not knowing number of
> warmup iterations?

Then you don't know when to stop the adaptation, and you get the adaptation window misalignment we had discussed earlier.

> It'd be nice to have time per iteration estimators
> even for the fixed number of iterations so we
> can estimate time remaining.   I think it'd be nice
> to be able to see iteration number, percentage
> iterations complete, log probability, and
> estimated time remaining.

Wouldn't be too hard -- add to the to-do?

> As far as estimating time per iteration,
> it might vary pretty widely during warmup, so
> I'm not sure how stable it will be and when we
> can do this.  Especially in the regime Andrew
> imagines where you intentially start out at a point
> that's likely to be too little time to converge.
>
> Even after convergence, there can be a lot of
> variation in tree depth explored (and hence time
> taken per iteration).

Sure, I don't disagree.  But the total time to convergence can also vary dramatically, which is at odds with sampling for only a preset amount of time.  Just thinking of ideas to try and do as best as possible given somewhat dissonant requirements.

messages.body_plain:
I'm glad you caught this before we had a host of
befuddled users.  I just pushed a fix.

I was mistakenly checking that the index j was a
proper parameter and I should've just been checking
the expression.  I was also doing the wrong thing for
binary and unary operators, so I fixed that, too.

I don't like how the indexing is printing.  I should
probably have an "as written by user" expression
printer.  Right now, it prints the generated C++,
which can be ugly, e.g., get_base1(y2,j,"y2",1)
instead of y2[j].

- Bob

Marcus

The makefile needs to be updated to point to the new version of eigen
(3.1.3).  The commands there point to the old version, 3.1.2 which was
recently upgraded.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sun, Apr 28, 2013 at

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command options & adaptation for Metropolis
messages.body_plain:
On 4/28/13 3:05 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> What's the issue with not knowing number of
>> warmup iterations?
>
> Then you don't know when to stop the adaptation, and you get the adaptation window misalignment we had discussed earlier.

Can we do something like a moving average type adaptation where
old information dies out in strength over time?  Then there'd be
no discretization of the epochs for training covariance during
warmup.

I'd think it'd be easy to add to Welford's algorithm by adjusting
the ratio in the updates to do some past discounting.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 4/28/13 3:49 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Is it possible to avoid issuing the warning when only certain
> functions are called?  E.G., right now in one of my models I get a
> bunch of warnings that look like:
>
> Warning (non-fatal):     sampling statement (~) contains a transformed
> parameter or local variable.
>       You must increment lp__ with the log absolute determinant of the
> Jacobian of the transform.
>       Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
>            col(g,gaitI) ~ normal_log(...)

We know the semantics of col() just does indexing,
so we should be able to create a symbol table of
excluded functions.  But then we need to still check
inside them, because we can have usages like col(g/2, i).

For now, I think it might be better to just table this
warning message, as it's turning out to be more complicated
than I bargained for.

Program analysis is hard with a complex language!

- Bob

messages.subject: time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
messages.body_plain:
For estimating mass matrices for HMC and covar matrices
for Metropolis, we now use batches divided exponentially
like follows:

   51--100, 101--200, 201--400, 401--800

I'm not sure what we do if the user specifies 735
warmup iterations.  Mike had a suggestion to divide
it as 735/2^N.

But what do we do with adaptation for a fixed time?
Then we don't know the magic number 735 ahead of time.

One solution would be to just two accumulators.
There's a current accumulator.  It starts accumulating
sufficient stats at iteration 51.  At iteration 101,
the accumulator is made the old accumulator and a new
one is started.  At iteration 200, the current accumulator
is made the old one and a new one's started and so on.

Then if we stop short, we can just add the old and current
accumulators for the final result.

We could even add the accumulators as we went if the
solver's not too expensive.

We could even use the pair of accumulators to turn off
adaptation early if the mass matrix estimated for the previous
batch is similar to that for the current batch.  Of course,
that only checks that mass matrix estimation has stabilized,
not that we've reached the typical set.

- Bob

>>
>> Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
>> reason we're doing a batched estimator like this?  Strictly speaking
>> we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
>> continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
>> converges.  (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
>> Rosenthals work.)  It seems like that would be the simplest approach.
>
>
> I suggested the reverse -- downweighting old samples rather
> than downweighting new samples.

Actually "diminishing adaption" would be achieved by simply weighting
all samples equally, as the adaption of the resulting proposal
distribution would diminish over time as the estimate of the
covariance matrix converged.  Downweighting of older samples may
violate diminishing adaption, I haven't checked thoroughly.

I guess the point here is that I don't fully understand the nature of
the adaption we're trying to do here.  There is a (relatively)
standard adaptive form of (Gauss) Metropolis which is something like:

1) Compute sample covariance S of all previous iterations.
2) Use covariance matrix S to construct proposal distribution, e.g.,
p(x_t+1 | x_t, S) = N(x_t+1 | x_t, c S).
3) Use proposal distribution with Metropolis-Hastings accept-reject decision.

I've used this with relatively good success on problems where the
gradients were not available.  It's actually really easy to implement
and, with a few variations (regularize the estimate of S using a Inv
Wishart prior, use a mixture model with a "small variance" proposal
component, etc), can be made extremely robust.

It sounds like we're trying to do something very different though.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
> For estimating mass matrices for HMC and covar matrices
> for Metropolis, we now use batches divided exponentially
> like follows:
>
>  51--100, 101--200, 201--400, 401--800
>
> I'm not sure what we do if the user specifies 735
> warmup iterations.  Mike had a suggestion to divide
> it as 735/2^N.

Actually with the push I made yesterday the last batch "snaps" to the total number of warm-up samples.

> But what do we do with adaptation for a fixed time?
> Then we don't know the magic number 735 ahead of time.

I think the more fundamental issue is given a fixed time how do we figure out how to split the time between warmup and sampling.  Once we have a criterion for such a splitting incorporating adaptation shouldn't be too hard.  Not to say that I have any idea what a good criterion would be (yesterday I was throwing around time/sample estimation to convert the fixed time into fixed samples and appeal to our usual approach).

> Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
> reason we're doing a batched estimator like this?  Strictly speaking
> we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
> continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
> converges.  (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
> Rosenthals work.)  It seems like that would be the simplest approach.

I'm just using this particular batch approach for historical reasons, but we definitely need some form of forgetting.

The problem is that we're adapting to a moving target: the current state of the Markov chain.  If we just used a diminishing estimator the result would be highly biased by the initial samples which are likely to be drawn far from the typical set.  Because we only adapt during warmup we don't need to appeal to Rosenthal's work, but we could always add diminishing adaptation if it were so desired provided it's paired with some form of forgetting.

Now the easiest form of a forgetful adaptation would be a moving average, but I fear that HMC would force the vulnerabilities of a moving average.  The problem is that often HMC converges really, really fast and only the first few samples are outside of the typical set.  Those samples are really far outside the typical set, however, and effectively serve as outliers that pull the expectations further than they should.  Having a batch after which no previous samples are used helps to mitigate such outliers.

This all suggest a more robust warm-up procedure.  Because we don't want to adapt until we've hit the typical set (or are at least close to it), we could run a unit-metric trajectory a few times to deal with approximate convergence, then introduce an adaptive stage that handles learning the metric as well as finishing the convergence.  We could also abandon HMC considerations and use funkier trajectories (apply the NUTS criterion without a binary tree, for example, or terminate trajectories once they start regaining energy).  We've discussed it before and I have some ideas, but haven't had any chance to play with them given all of the refactoring for R-HMC.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
messages.body_plain:
The method outlined above is effectively the "Adaptive Metropolis"
described by Roberts and Rosenthal in section 2 of
http://probability.ca/jeff/ftpdir/adaptex.pdf

The question is what you actually expect the sampler to adapt to?
With a windowed, moving or discounted estimate you'll get local
estimates of curvature, but you'll always have to stop the adaption
before you can draw any real samples.  Then the question is what
covariance estimate do you use for the non-warmup samples?  The last
window which is only good locally or a global estimate?  Local
estimates will be strongly stuck in a single region and give highly
confident but potentially inaccurate estimates.

I would suggest that with most methods (excluding things like RMHMC)
the only thing you can hope for is to adapt to the global covariance
structure, in which case you might as well continue adapting
indefinitely (or until it's numerically converged).  Early iterations
can be ignored, but in my experience their impact tends to be
relatively quickly forgotten.

That said, different approaches may be called for between HMC and Metropolis.

Cheers,
Marcus

The simplest idea was to specify time t.
Warmup, terminating with the first iteration ending after
time t/2.  Then sample, terminating after time t.

There was some discussion about whether to have a minimum
number of samples (split-R-hat needs at least 4, I think,
to avoid a zero in denominator of the variance estimate).

I don't know that there's any deeper motivation for
Andrew wanting to split time and number of samples other
than it bounds the time (or iterations) wasted adapting
after convergence during warmup.

R-hat's easy enough to do online, but split R-hat isn't.
But you could do it in batches.

We could also specify running for a max of time t and a max
of K iterations.  That would terminate warmup after K/2
iterations if it occurs before t/2 and terminate sampling
after K total iterations if it occurs before time t.

- Bob

> I don't know that there's any deeper motivation for

My main motivation was convenience. As a user, I want to just run and get some results.  Running for 2 minutes (or 20 minutes, whatever) makes sense, running until approx convergence makes sense, running until n_eff>100 (or 1000, whatever) makes sense.  But running 1000 iterations doesn't make sense to me.  There's nothing special about an iteration.  And I think people have been trained by Bugs to pick huge numbers of iterations.

Then, after we discussed this, we realized there is a potential feature/bug that different chains will have different numbers of iterations.

>
> R-hat's easy enough to do online, but split R-hat isn't.
> But you could do it in batches.

Split R-hat is of course just one way to do it.  Perhaps we can create some online-computable thing that does the job.  That would be cool.

That's just the "why time"?  The question is why half
the time in warmup and half sampling, or half the iterations
on warmup and half sampling?

Ideally we'd want "warmup until I converge" and "sample
until I get (split) R-hat below 1+epsilon and n_eff > tau".

No idea how to measure convergence during warmup other
than that the covariance or mass matrix estimator converges.
And if we could measure it effectively, we might not need
R-hat at all.  We could then just run until large enough
n_eff.

I think Michael may have had some ideas on how to measure
whether you hit the typical set...

> Split R-hat is of course just one way to do it.  Perhaps we can create some online-computable thing that does the job.  That would be cool.

I think we can run a kind of split R-hat that may
not be perfectly balanced that would work efficiently for
an unpredictable numbers of iterations.  Like what we've
been talking about doing for mass/covar matrix estimation.
We can talk about  it tomorrow.
